opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to break this down into a few pieces.

When we first get AIs that can fully automate AI research, meaning you could basically replace the research staff at a frontier lab with AI systems, I'd guess the initial speedup isn't astronomical. Maybe something like a several-fold increase in the rate of algorithmic progress, though there's a lot of uncertainty there. A big reason it's not immediately enormous is compute bottlenecks. You can have a huge number of very fast, very capable AI researchers, but they still need to run experiments, and experiments eat compute. So you get diminishing returns from throwing more cognitive labor at a fixed compute budget.

Then the question is what happens over the following months. There's a feedback loop: the AIs improve algorithms, which makes the AIs better and cheaper to run, which means you have more and smarter AI researchers, which speeds up progress further. Whether that loop accelerates or fizzles depends a lot on how fast returns to research effort diminish. Basically, does each doubling of algorithmic efficiency get harder to find faster than your research capacity grows? My sense is it's fairly plausible, maybe somewhere around a coin flip or a bit less, that you get a progressively accelerating software-only takeoff for some period, before you run into hard limits.

So within the first year, I could imagine you go from that initial several-fold speedup to something considerably larger, possibly compressing what would otherwise be many years of algorithmic progress into a year or less. But I'd also put real weight on scenarios where it's more like a steady but elevated rate, because compute constraints keep binding and the low-hanging fruit gets picked.

There are some other factors too. Early on, the AIs might be superhuman at some research tasks and weaker at others, like research taste, picking which directions to pursue. If taste improves rapidly, that could be a big multiplier, because a lot of research efficiency comes from not wasting compute on dumb experiments. And there's the question of how aggressively the lab is actually going. A lab that's racing will try to capture as much of that speedup as possible, whereas a more cautious actor might deliberately slow down to do safety work.

From a safety perspective, that's what worries me. If you're going from roughly human-level research automation to something vastly superhuman in under a year, there's very little time to notice problems, figure out whether your alignment and control measures are holding up, and course-correct. So I think it's quite important to prepare in advance for a world where that first year moves very fast, even if it's not certain it will.

r001.rationale: It says the initial speedup could grow over the following months through a feedback loop, potentially accelerating progress.

r002.rationale: It suggests a year could compress many years of progress, but does not say that most first-year progress could occur in the first six months.

r003.rationale: It discusses diminishing returns and low-hanging fruit, but does not attribute early concentration of first-year progress to diminishing returns setting in quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that when you first get something like fully automated AI R&D — meaning an AI system that can basically do everything a top researcher at an AI company could do, just as a drop-in replacement — you don't instantly get the full speedup. There's a ramp.

My rough picture is that at the start, maybe you're getting something like a 3x to 5x speedup on the overall rate of algorithmic progress. And the reason it's not higher right from day one is a few things. One is that you're bottlenecked on compute — experiments still take as long to run as they did before, and a lot of the work of AI research is actually waiting on GPUs. So you can be much smarter about which experiments to run, and you can run many more small-scale experiments and extrapolate, but you can't just make the big training runs go faster. Another is that the organization has to adapt. You've got human researchers who are used to working one way, and now you have maybe millions of parallel instances of a system running at ten or fifty times human speed, and figuring out how to actually direct that effectively, and how to trust its outputs, takes time. There's a bunch of operational friction.

But then the key dynamic is that the AI is improving the AI. So once you're at a 3x speedup, the AIs are working on making the next generation of AIs better, and that generation is more capable, and so the speedup goes up. And I think it could plausibly go from something like 3x to something more like 10x, or even 20x or 30x, over the course of the first year. Though I want to be clear there's huge uncertainty here — I could easily see it being more like 2x and stalling out because compute really is the binding constraint, or I could see it going a lot faster than that.

The other thing I'd flag is that the speedup isn't uniform across types of work. Things that are purely cognitive — coming up with ideas, writing code, debugging, analyzing results — those can get accelerated enormously, like 10x, 50x almost immediately. Things that are bound by physical processes, running the actual training, building chips, those barely move at first. So the effective overall speedup is kind of a weighted average, and over the first year a lot of what's happening is the AIs finding ways to route around the compute bottleneck — better experimental methodology, more sample-efficient training, getting more out of each FLOP. And how well that works is really the crux for how fast the first year goes.

r001.rationale: It says the speedup could rise from roughly 3× at the start to 10×, 20×, or 30× over the first year.

r002.rationale: It gives a possible increase over the first year but does not say that most research progress could happen within the first six months.

r003.rationale: It attributes the possible increase to AI improving AI and discusses compute limits, but does not attribute early concentration of progress to diminishing returns setting in quickly.

astra-6.text:
I’d expect it to change quite a lot over that year, rather than being a fixed multiplier. Initially, you might automate a bunch of relatively straightforward work, but still have humans deciding which experiments to run and interpreting the results. So even if the AI is very fast at writing code, the overall research process might only get somewhat faster.

Then the question is how quickly you remove those remaining bottlenecks. If the systems become good at choosing research directions, running experiments, and figuring out what to do next, you could get a much larger speedup. And there’s a feedback loop: faster AI research produces better AIs, which can do more of the research.

But I wouldn’t assume that translates into a smooth exponential curve. Experiments still take time, compute is limited, and some improvements are much harder to find than others. So I’d put substantial uncertainty on where you end up after a year. The key distinction is between automating individual tasks and automating the whole research process.

r001.rationale: It contrasts modest initial acceleration with a potentially much larger speedup as systems take over more of the research process, and describes a feedback loop that improves AI research.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate that most first-year progress could occur in the first six months.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute early-concentrated progress to diminishing returns setting in quickly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you should expect the speedup to change quite a lot over that year. You might initially have systems that can automate some coding and run experiments, but still need humans to decide which experiments are worth doing and interpret the results. That could be a substantial productivity boost without making the whole research process dramatically faster.

Then, as the systems improve, they might start taking over more of those other parts. And there’s a feedback loop: better systems accelerate the research that produces the next generation of systems, which can accelerate research further.

But I wouldn’t assume that this translates directly into an explosion. You can run into bottlenecks from compute, the time experiments take, or figuring out whether a proposed improvement actually works. If you generate ten times as many ideas but can’t test them much faster, that limits the benefit.

So I’d distinguish the initial speedup from how quickly that speedup itself increases. A fairly modest initial effect could become very large over a year if the remaining bottlenecks are things the systems can help remove. If those bottlenecks are harder to address, you could instead get a substantial boost that stays relatively stable. I’m quite uncertain about which trajectory we should expect.

r001.rationale: The response says a modest initial speedup could become very large over the year as systems improve and accelerate further research.

r002.rationale: It does not say that most research progress in many models would occur in the first six months.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute any early concentration of progress to diminishing returns setting in quickly.
